oneSentence: The ability of a model to give useful results on new cases, not just on the examples used to build or tune it.
plainExplanation:
A model is built from past examples, often called training data. Generalisation asks whether its performance carries over to relevant examples it has not seen before.

Testing does not create generalisation. It provides evidence about it. Developers compare predictions with known answers on a separate set of examples. Strong performance on relevant unseen data suggests better generalisation. A sharp drop suggests that patterns learned during development do not transfer well.

Accuracy and generalisation are not the same. Accuracy is a measurement on a particular dataset. Generalisation concerns performance beyond the data used to train or tune the model. A model can have high development accuracy and still perform poorly in practice.

Generalisation also differs from memorisation and overfitting. Memorisation means repeating training examples or narrow patterns. Overfitting occurs when fitting the training examples closely leads to worse performance on new cases. Generalisation is usually estimated with held-out test data or cross-validation, followed by checks under relevant operating conditions.

everydayAnalogy.title: Using the map, not memorising the route
everydayAnalogy.story: Someone practises cycling to one address until every turn is familiar. That does not show they can reach a new address. If they have learned to read the map, recognise street signs and adjust when a road is closed, they can handle routes they have not practised. A model generalises when it likewise applies what it learned to new, relevant cases rather than merely reproducing familiar patterns.

Also, library wings may follow one clear catalogue rule, while real-world data can shift in messier ways, with hidden changes in language, sensors, populations or behaviour.

visual.title: Good score on familiar data vs good performance on new data
visual.learningObjective: Show why a model must be checked on fresh data to tell whether it will work beyond development examples.
visual.description: A two-column comparison. The left column shows a model evaluated on the same kind of data it learned from and getting a high score. The right column shows the same model on separate, unseen data, where the score either stays strong or drops. Read top to bottom in each column, then compare the final boxes.

steps.label: Build from past examples
steps.explanation: The model is developed using labelled examples from one dataset.
steps.visualInstruction: Top row spanning both columns: draw a box labelled 'training data' feeding into a box labelled 'model built and tuned'.

steps.label: Check on familiar-style data
steps.explanation: A score measured on data very similar to development data can look impressive, but it does not prove broader usefulness.
steps.visualInstruction: Left column middle: arrow from 'model built and tuned' to a box labelled 'evaluation close to development data'; below it, a green score badge.

steps.label: Check on unseen data
steps.explanation: Use separate examples the model did not train on to test whether performance carries over.
steps.visualInstruction: Right column middle: arrow from 'model built and tuned' to a box labelled 'held-out or new data'; below it, a score badge.

steps.label: Compare the outcomes
steps.explanation: If performance stays good on unseen data, generalisation looks better. If it falls sharply, the model may not transfer well.
steps.visualInstruction: Bottom row: left result box says 'looks good here'; right result box splits into two small outcomes: 'score stays similar' and 'score drops'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each result box to reveal a short note: 'similar score suggests better generalisation' or 'large drop suggests poor generalisation or mismatch between datasets'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This comparison diagram explains that generalisation is about performance on new data, not just development data. First, training data is used to build and tune a model. Then two evaluations are shown. In the left column, the model is tested on data very similar to what it learned from, and it gets a high score. In the right column, the model is tested on held-out or new data it did not train on. If the score stays similar, that suggests better generalisation. If the score drops a lot, that suggests poor generalisation or a mismatch between datasets. The main lesson is that a strong score in familiar conditions is not enough.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column comparison with the same boxes and labels, no animation. Notes that would appear on hover are shown as small text under each outcome.

workedExample.scenario: The officer tests whether the classifier can recognise access constraints in field updates it did not encounter during development.
workedExample.input: A development set of earlier updates and a separate, later batch kept out of training and tuning.
process: The classifier is fitted and tuned only on the development set, where its precision and recall appear strong.
The later batch remains untouched until the final evaluation, preventing information from the test material leaking into development.
On the held-out batch, recall drops because several sources describe access constraints using different shorthand and sentence structures.
The officer examines the missed cases and checks whether the gap reflects overfitting, limited data coverage or a change in reporting patterns.
workedExample.result: The lower performance on held-out updates reveals a generalisation gap. Before operational use, the classifier needs broader development data and another evaluation on fresh material, not further tuning against the same test batch.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A humanitarian affairs officer in a country office is assessing a classifier that sorts incoming field updates by issue before preparing a briefing note for clearance at 6pm.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Strong results on updates used during development mean little if the classifier misses new wording, abbreviations or reporting styles. It should be evaluated on genuinely held-out updates from later periods and different sources, using measures that reflect the cost of missed or incorrect flags.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not enter raw field updates containing personal, protection-related or security-sensitive information into a tool that is not approved for such material. Evaluation must use an approved environment and appropriately minimised or de-identified data. Every flag still requires human review before it affects the briefing note or any follow-up.

whyItMatters: A system can look strong in a demo, a pilot or a benchmark and still fail in real use. Generalisation matters because most decisions rely on the future, not the past examples used to build the model. If a model does not generalise, people may trust scores that do not hold across places, time periods, languages or populations. That can waste money, miss important cases, or create unfair results. For a non-specialist, this term is a practical warning: ask not only 'What score did it get?' but also 'On what data, and does that resemble where we plan to use it?'

An evaluation office discussing whether model results transfer across reporting periods

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model has high accuracy, it generalises well.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Accuracy is only a score on a particular dataset. A model may score highly on data that is very similar to its training data, or on data affected by leakage, and still perform poorly on genuinely new cases.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Generalisation means the model works equally well for every group and setting.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Good generalisation usually means performance carries over better to new data overall, but that does not guarantee equal performance across languages, regions or subgroups. Those still need separate checks.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A very large training dataset automatically solves generalisation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: More data often helps, but only if the data is relevant and varied enough. If the data is narrow, unrepresentative or contains repeated patterns, a model can still fail on new situations.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: In simple terms, this means a model learned something useful that still helps on new examples, not just on the examples used to build it.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Technically, generalisation is the performance a fitted model is expected to achieve on relevant unseen data. The difference between development performance and unseen-data performance is the generalisation gap. Generalisation is estimated with held-out test sets or cross-validation, using metrics suited to the task, such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score or calibration. Poor unseen performance can result from overfitting, data leakage, distribution mismatch or evaluation procedures that do not reflect intended use. The central question is whether patterns fitted from the observed sample support useful performance beyond that sample.

keyTakeaway: Judge a model by useful performance on relevant cases it has not seen, not by how well it handles material used to build or tune it.

quickCheck.question: Which result is the best evidence that a model generalises well?
options: It scores highly on the same dataset used to train and tune it.
It keeps a similar level of performance on separate, unseen data from the intended use setting.
It gives confident answers very quickly.
It uses a very large number of parameters.
quickCheck.explanation: Generalisation is about whether performance carries over to new cases. A high score on training or tuning data can be misleading, and speed or model size does not show that the model will work well on unseen examples.

issues.problem: The sentence "What happens in between is testing" falsely presents testing as the process that produces generalisation. Testing only estimates how well a trained model performs on unseen data. The input-output framing is also misleading because generalisation is a property of performance, not a pipeline with old data as its input and a score as its output.

issues.problem: The definition equates generalisation with unseen performance matching development performance. That is wrong because equally poor performance on both datasets would produce a small gap without showing useful generalisation. Matching scores describes the generalisation gap, not generalisation itself.

issues.problem: The visual contrasts "familiar-style data" with unseen data, but these are not opposites. Proper held-out data is often deliberately similar to development data while still being unseen. The diagram therefore blurs whether it is teaching separation from training data or robustness to a changed setting.
issues.fix: Revise the columns to contrast evaluation on data used during development with evaluation on separate, unseen data. Treat changed settings as an additional check, not as the definition of unseen data.

issues.problem: The claim that the model "does not generalise well enough" is unsupported because no acceptable performance threshold is given. The arithmetic itself is consistent: 95% of 10,000 is 9,500, and 74% of 2,000 is 1,480. The justified conclusion is that performance fell substantially, not that 74% is necessarily inadequate.
issues.fix: The model’s performance falls substantially on fresh data. Its strong development score did not carry over, so the team should investigate data coverage, evaluation and possibly a different approach.

issues.problem: Option 1 says only that performance remains similar. Similar but poor performance would not satisfy the page’s definition of useful generalisation. Options 2 and 3 are also implausible distractors, making the answer obvious without much understanding. Option 0 is not evidence because it uses training and tuning data. Option 1 is the intended answer but needs to require strong performance. Speed and parameter count in options 2 and 3 provide no evidence of generalisation.
issues.fix: Replace options 1 to 3 with: "It keeps strong performance on separate, unseen data from the intended use setting."; "It scores well on a selected test set."; "It was tuned until its test score improved." Keep correctOptionIndex as 1. Explain that strong performance on separate unseen data is the relevant evidence, while selected or repeatedly reused evaluation data can mislead.
